questions.question: Hunger strike as a weapon was used for the first time by Mahatma Gandhi during which struggle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Struggle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi used the hunger strike for the first time during the **Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Struggle** of 1918.
 
• The strike was initiated to demand **better wages and working conditions** for the mill workers.
 
• Gandhi's hunger strike was a non-violent method to support the workers and exert moral pressure on mill owners.
 
• The dispute revolved around the mill owners refusing to grant a** 50% wage hike** as compensation for the increased cost of living during World War I.
 
• Gandhi's intervention and hunger strike led to a peaceful resolution, with the workers achieving a **35% wage increase**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hunger Strike:**

 
 
• A non-violent method of protest where individuals refuse to eat to draw attention to a cause or demand justice.
 
• This method was frequently used by Gandhi as part of his philosophy of **Satyagraha** (truth-force).
 
 
 
• **Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Struggle:**
 
 
• It was one of the first significant labor movements in India led by Gandhi.
 
• The strike was a pivotal moment in India's labor rights history and demonstrated the power of peaceful protest.
 
 
 
• **Satyagraha:**
 
 
• A philosophy and practice of nonviolent resistance developed by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• It emphasizes the power of truth and nonviolence in achieving justice and social change.
 
 
 
• **Gandhi's Leadership in Labor Movements:**
 
 
• Besides the Ahmedabad strike, Gandhi also supported workers during the **Champaran Satyagraha** (indigo farmers) and **Kheda Satyagraha** (peasants).
 
• His efforts helped establish workers' rights as an essential aspect of India's freedom struggle.

questions.question: The Badami caves in Karnataka have been built by which of the following rulers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chalukyas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Badami Caves, located in Karnataka, were built during the reign of the **Chalukyas**, specifically under the rule of Pulakeshin I and his successors.
 
• These caves are primarily dedicated to Hindu deities like Shiva and Vishnu, along with some Jain influences, showcasing the religious diversity of the era.
 
• The rock-cut architecture of Badami caves highlights the **Dravidian style** with intricate carvings and sculptures.
 
• Badami served as the capital of the early Chalukya dynasty during the 6th to 8th centuries, symbolizing their architectural prowess.
 
• There are four main cave temples at Badami, which are a mix of **Hindu and Jain traditions**, reflecting the cultural synthesis of the Chalukya period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chalukya Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Chalukyas ruled a significant part of southern and central India between the 6th and 12th centuries.
 
• They are divided into three branches: Early Chalukyas of Badami, Later Chalukyas of Kalyani, and Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi.
 
• The dynasty was known for its patronage of art, architecture, and literature.
 
 
 
• **Rock-Cut Architecture:**
 
 
• Rock-cut temples are structures carved directly into natural rocks, showcasing advanced craftsmanship.
 
• The Badami caves are prime examples of rock-cut architecture, featuring intricate carvings and sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Dravidian Style of Architecture:**
 
 
• Originating in South India, Dravidian architecture is characterized by pyramid-shaped temples, intricate sculptures, and carvings.
 
• The Badami caves reflect early Dravidian architectural elements, which influenced later temple constructions.
 
 
 
• **Religious Significance:**
 
 
• The cave temples are dedicated to Hindu deities like Shiva and Vishnu, with Jain influences in some caves.
 
• They highlight the religious harmony and cultural synthesis during the Chalukya period.

questions.question:

2. It offers direct annual cash transfers of ₹1 lakh to selected SHG members to support their livelihoods.

The correct answer is __**Option 3: 1 and 3**__.

• The 'Lakhpati Didi' scheme aims to **empower women by enabling members of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) to achieve an annual household income of at least ₹1 lakh**, sustained through agricultural seasons or business cycles.
 
• The scheme is implemented under the **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)**, which is spearheaded by the Ministry of Rural Development.
 
• It focuses on enhancing the livelihoods of rural women through entrepreneurial activities, capacity building, and access to financial resources.
 
• The scheme does not include direct annual cash transfers of ₹1 lakh to beneficiaries, but instead supports income generation via skill development and enterprise promotion.
 
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacted with the beneficiaries of the scheme in Gujarat in March 2025 to assess its impact on women empowerment and rural development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Launched in 2011, DAY-NRLM aims to reduce poverty by enhancing sustainable livelihood opportunities for rural poor households.
 
• It focuses on creating efficient and effective institutional platforms for the rural poor, especially women, to enable them to increase household income through self-employment and skilled wage employment opportunities.
 
• The mission promotes financial inclusion by linking SHGs to banks for credit support.
 
 
 
• **Self-Help Groups (SHGs):**
 
 
• SHGs are small, voluntary associations of people, typically women, who come together to save and collectively manage resources for income-generating activities.
 
• They play a significant role in empowering women and improving rural livelihoods.
 
 
 
• **Empowerment of Women through SHGs:**
 
 
• SHGs facilitate access to credit, skills training, and market linkages, enabling women to start and sustain micro-enterprises.
 
• The 'Lakhpati Didi' scheme is a prime example of leveraging SHGs for women’s economic empowerment.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of DAY-NRLM:**
 
 
• Universal social mobilization by bringing at least one woman from each identified rural poor household into SHG networks.
 
• Skill development and entrepreneurship promotion to enhance employability and income generation.

questions.question: Which industries commonly used Tetrachloromethane as a degreasing agent?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Manufacturing and mechanical industries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride)** is commonly utilized in manufacturing and mechanical industries due to its excellent degreasing properties.
 
• This compound is effective in removing grease, oil, and other contaminants from metal surfaces, tools, and machinery.
 
• Mechanical industries employ it for cleaning parts during assembly, maintenance, and repair tasks.
 
• Its non-flammable nature made it a preferred choice in industrial applications before its usage was restricted due to environmental concerns.
 
• Industries like aerospace and automotive heavily relied on Tetrachloromethane for degreasing metal components.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tetrachloromethane (Carbon Tetrachloride):**

 
 
• A chemical compound with the formula CCl₄.
 
• Historically used as a solvent, cleaning agent, and refrigerant.
 
• Its use has significantly declined due to its adverse health effects and contribution to ozone layer depletion.
 
 
 
• **Degreasing Agents:**
 
 
• Chemical substances used to remove grease, oil, or dirt from surfaces.
 
• Examples include organic solvents, alkaline solutions, and detergents.
 
• They are widely applied in industries for cleaning machinery, tools, and metal parts.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• Carbon Tetrachloride is classified as a potent ozone-depleting substance under the Montreal Protocol.
 
• Its production and use have been phased out in many countries due to its harmful environmental effects.
 
• It is also considered a hazardous air pollutant with serious health risks to humans.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Degreasing Solutions:**
 
 
• Eco-friendly alternatives include water-based cleaners and biodegradable solvents.
 
• Industries are increasingly adopting non-toxic and sustainable cleaning agents.
 
• These alternatives help reduce health risks and environmental impact.

questions.question: Labour reforms have remained a key agenda in the post-1991 economic policy landscape. How many labour codes were consolidated by the Indian government under the labour reforms enacted in 2019-2020?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Four**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian government consolidated 29 existing labour laws into **four labour codes** as part of labour reforms enacted in 2019-2020.
 
• The four labour codes are: **Code on Wages, Code on Industrial Relations, Code on Social Security, and Code on Occupational Safety, Health, and Working Conditions**.
 
• These reforms aim to simplify, modernize, and streamline labour regulations, ensuring ease of compliance and promoting labour welfare.
 
• The consolidation addresses issues such as outdated provisions, multiplicity of definitions, and overlapping jurisdictions, which often created confusion and inefficiencies.
 
• The labour codes provide a uniform framework for both workers and employers, promoting transparency and fostering a conducive environment for economic growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Code on Wages, 2019:**

 
 
• This code subsumes four wage-related laws, including the Payment of Wages Act and Minimum Wages Act.
 
• It ensures a statutory minimum wage across all sectors and simplifies wage-related compliance.
 
 
 
• **Code on Industrial Relations, 2020:**
 
 
• It aims to balance the rights of employers and employees, facilitating better industrial relations.
 
• Provisions include streamlined dispute resolution mechanisms and conditions for strikes and lockouts.
 
 
 
• **Code on Social Security, 2020:**
 
 
• This code integrates nine laws related to social security, such as the Employees' Provident Fund and Maternity Benefit Act.
 
• It expands the social security net to cover gig and platform workers.
 
 
 
• **Code on Occupational Safety, Health, and Working Conditions, 2020:**
 
 
• This code combines 13 laws related to health, safety, and working conditions.
 
• It focuses on ensuring safe working environments and welfare provisions for workers in various industries.
 
 
 
• **Objective of Labour Reforms:**
 
 
• The reforms aim to enhance the ease of doing business and attract investments while safeguarding workers' rights.
 
• They are crucial for creating a flexible, simplified, and transparent labour regulatory framework in India.

questions.question: What happens when you press 'Enter' while working with a bullet or numbered list in MS Word 365?

options.text: It converts the list into plain text.
It deletes the previous bullet or number.
It creates a new list item with the same bullet or number.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It creates a new list item with the same bullet or number.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When you press **‘Enter’** while working with a bullet or numbered list in MS Word 365, it automatically creates a **new list item with the same bullet or numbering style**.
 
• The newly created bullet or number appears directly below the previous item, maintaining the same formatting style.
 
• If the user presses **‘Enter’ twice**, the current list is terminated, and the cursor moves to a new line without any bullets or numbering.
 
• This functionality is part of the **auto-formatting features** of MS Word, designed to streamline the creation of lists and improve efficiency in document editing.
 
• Users can also customize the bullet or numbering style by accessing the **‘Bullets and Numbering’** menu in the toolbar.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bullets and Numbering in MS Word:**

 
 
• Bullets are used for unordered lists, while numbering is used for ordered lists.
 
• The user can access these options under the **‘Home’ tab** in the toolbar.
 
• Customizing bullets or numbering allows for the use of symbols, images, or different number formats.
 
 
 
• **Keyboard Shortcuts for Lists:**
 
 
• Pressing **‘Ctrl + Shift + L’** applies a default bullet style to the selected text.
 
• To increase or decrease the indentation level of a list, use **‘Tab’** or **‘Shift + Tab’**, respectively.
 
 
 
• **Auto-Formatting Features:**
 
 
• MS Word auto-detects list patterns when typing (e.g., starting a line with "1." or "-").
 
• This feature can be toggled on/off in the **‘AutoCorrect Options’** under the ‘File’ menu.
 
 
 
• **Ending a List:**
 
 
• Pressing **‘Enter’ twice** ends the current list and moves the cursor to a new line without bullets or numbering.
 
• Alternatively, users can manually remove bullets or numbering by clicking the respective icons in the toolbar.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Cultural and educational rights are fundamental rights.
These are subject to reasonable restriction.
These may be enforced by the courts.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**These are absolute.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are **not absolute**; they are subject to reasonable restrictions to ensure public order, morality, and national security.
 
• **Article 19(2)** of the Constitution explicitly mentions reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression.
 
• The Fundamental Rights are enforceable by the courts under **Article 32**, which provides the right to constitutional remedies.
 
• The Constitution grants **Cultural and Educational Rights** as Fundamental Rights under Articles 29 and 30 to protect minority groups.
 
• While Fundamental Rights are guaranteed, they can be suspended during a national emergency as stated under **Article 359**, except for Articles 20 and 21.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, spanning Articles 12 to 35.
 
• They ensure the basic rights and freedoms of individuals, including equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, and religious freedom.
 
• They are classified into six categories: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:**
 
 
• Restrictions are imposed to maintain public order, morality, health, security, and friendly relations with foreign states.
 
• Such restrictions are defined within the Constitution and upheld by judicial review to prevent misuse by authorities.
 
 
 
• **Article 32 - Right to Constitutional Remedies:**
 
 
• Referred to as the "heart and soul of the Constitution" by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• Allows individuals to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Empowers courts to issue writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari.
 
 
 
• **Suspension of Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• During a national emergency under Article 352, certain Fundamental Rights can be suspended.
 
• Rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even in emergencies.
 
• Article 358 and Article 359 specify conditions for suspension during emergencies.

questions.question: Which keyboard shortcut is typically used to paste copied content?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ctrl + V**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ctrl + V** is the standard keyboard shortcut used to paste content in most operating systems and applications.
 
• This shortcut works universally across platforms like Windows, macOS, and Linux, making it a widely recognized function.
 
• It is part of the trio of common shortcuts: **Ctrl + C (copy), Ctrl + X (cut), and Ctrl + V (paste)**.
 
• The use of "V" for pasting can be traced back to early computer systems, where it was chosen because "P" was already assigned to "Print."
 
• The shortcut is supported by most text editors, word processors, and graphical user interfaces for efficient and quick workflow.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Keyboard Shortcuts**

 
 
• Keyboard shortcuts are combinations of keys that provide quick access to specific functions within a software or operating system.
 
• They help improve productivity by reducing the need for mouse interactions.
 
• Examples include **Ctrl + Z** (undo), **Ctrl + Y** (redo), and **Ctrl + A** (select all).
 
 
 
• **Clipboard**
 
 
• The clipboard is a temporary storage area used to transfer data between documents or applications.
 
• When you use **Ctrl + C** or **Ctrl + X**, the data is saved to the clipboard until you paste it using **Ctrl + V**.
 
• Modern operating systems often support clipboard history, allowing users to access multiple copied items.
 
 
 
• **History of Ctrl + V**
 
 
• The shortcut system was popularized by Xerox PARC in the 1970s and later adopted by Apple and Microsoft.
 
• Early systems like Apple Lisa and Macintosh standardized these shortcuts, which were later incorporated into Windows.
 
 
 
• **Cross-Platform Usage**
 
 
• On macOS, the equivalent shortcut for paste is **Cmd + V**.
 
• Linux-based systems also follow the **Ctrl + V** convention, though terminal applications may use different shortcuts.

questions.question: In which year was the Right to Property removed from the Fundamental Rights of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1978**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Right to Property was originally included as a Fundamental Right under **Article 19(1)(f)** and Article 31 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978**, during the tenure of Prime Minister Morarji Desai.
 
• After the amendment, the Right to Property was reclassified as a **legal right** under Article 300A in Part XII of the Constitution.
 
• The change was made to resolve conflicts between private property rights and the government's power to acquire land for public purposes.
 
• This amendment curtailed the misuse of property-related rights and allowed the government greater flexibility in enacting land reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**:

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by courts.
 
• Initially, there were seven Fundamental Rights, but now there are six after the removal of the Right to Property.
 
 
 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978**:
 
 
• This was enacted to nullify some provisions of the 42nd Amendment, which was passed during the Emergency period (1975-77).
 
• It ensured that Fundamental Rights could not be easily abridged or suspended except during a properly declared emergency.
 
 
 
• **Article 300A**:
 
 
• It states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by the authority of law.
 
• It made the Right to Property a statutory (legal) right instead of a Fundamental Right.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Change**:
 
 
• Reclassification of the Right to Property helped the government implement land acquisition and agrarian reforms more effectively.
 
• It reduced the number of property-related litigations in courts.

questions.question: What is used along with milk to distill the Pithora colours in Pithora painting?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahuda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mahuda (Madhuca longifolia)** is a vital ingredient used in Pithora painting to distill natural pigments for creating the vibrant colors used in this art form.
 
• Mahuda flowers are mixed with milk to create a liquid medium that helps extract the natural colors from organic pigments.
 
• It is a traditional method employed by the Rathwa and Bhil tribes of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, who are renowned for Pithora paintings.
 
• The use of Mahuda ensures that the colors maintain their natural vibrancy and adhere well to the surface of the walls.
 
• Mahuda is also culturally significant to these tribes, being used in various rituals and traditional practices, including its application in art.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pithora Painting**

 
 
• Pithora painting is a ritualistic and traditional art form of the Rathwa and Bhil tribes in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
 
• These paintings are typically created on the walls of houses to invoke blessings from the deity Pithora Baba for prosperity and well-being.
 
• They are vibrant depictions of tribal culture, incorporating animals, humans, and deities in a symbolic style.
 
 
 
• **Natural Pigments in Pithora Art**
 
 
• Natural pigments derived from organic materials such as rice paste, turmeric, and flowers are traditionally used in Pithora paintings.
 
• The colors are prepared using a mix of milk and Mahuda to ensure their durability and brightness.
 
 
 
• **Mahuda Tree (Madhuca longifolia)**
 
 
• Mahuda is a tropical tree native to India and is widely revered in tribal communities.
 
• The flowers of the tree are used in various applications, such as brewing traditional alcoholic beverages, cooking, and as a natural ingredient in art.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Milk in Pithora Painting**
 
 
• Milk is used as a binder in traditional Pithora art to create a smooth, adhesive medium for natural pigments.
 
• It symbolizes purity and is often associated with the sacred nature of the rituals connected to Pithora painting.

questions.question: Which financial institution was established by the 74th Constitutional Amendment, 1992, to review the finances of Urban Local Government Bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**State Finance Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992** mandated the establishment of the State Finance Commission (SFC) to review the financial position of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).
 
• The SFC is constituted by the respective **State Governments** every five years to recommend measures for improving the financial health of local self-governments.
 
• Its primary responsibility is to **distribute financial resources** between the state government and local bodies, ensuring adequate funding for developmental activities.
 
• The recommendations of the SFC include devolution of taxes, grants-in-aid, and improving revenue-generating capabilities of ULBs and PRIs.
 
• This initiative aligns with the spirit of **decentralization**, empowering local self-governments to perform their functions more effectively.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**

 
 
• This Act provided a constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in India.
 
• It introduced the concept of decentralized governance through institutions like Municipalities, Municipal Corporations, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• It also emphasized the importance of financial sustainability and accountability in local governance.
 
 
 
• **State Finance Commission (SFC)**
 
 
• The SFC was established under Article 243-I of the Constitution.
 
• It is responsible for reviewing the financial position of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies within the state.
 
• The SFC provides recommendations on tax assignments, revenue-sharing, and grants-in-aid for local bodies.
 
 
 
• **Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**
 
 
• ULBs are the governing institutions responsible for administering towns and cities in India.
 
• They include Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, and Nagar Panchayats, which are categorized based on the population size.
 
• ULBs are tasked with providing essential services such as water supply, sanitation, waste management, and urban planning.
 
 
 
• **Decentralization**
 
 
• Decentralization refers to the transfer of decision-making powers and responsibilities from central authorities to lower levels of government.
 
• It aims to improve governance, ensure participation, and enhance service delivery at the grassroots level.
 
• The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments are key milestones in India’s journey toward decentralized governance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of contract farming in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fixed buy-back rate by companies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Contract farming** involves an agreement between a farmer and a company (buyer) for the production and supply of agricultural products at predetermined prices.
 
• The agreement often includes a **fixed buy-back rate** for the produce, ensuring price stability for the farmers.
 
• It is a practice widely adopted to **reduce market risks for farmers** and ensure a steady supply of raw materials for companies.
 
• Contract farming provides access to **advanced technology, quality seeds, fertilizers, and technical knowledge** supplied by companies.
 
• It is a regulated practice under the **Indian Model Agricultural Produce and Livestock Contract Farming Act, 2018**, which protects the interests of both farmers and companies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Contract Farming Act, 2018:**

 
 
• This model act aims to promote contract farming by providing a framework for agreements between farmers and sponsors.
 
• It includes provisions to prevent exploitation of farmers, including **no transfer of land ownership** to sponsors.
 
• The act also ensures dispute resolution through a fast-track mechanism.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Contract Farming:**
 
 
• Farmers benefit from guaranteed pricing and reduced market risks.
 
• Companies ensure a steady supply of raw materials with desired quality standards.
 
• Farmers gain access to modern technology and better farming practices.
 
 
 
• **Disadvantages of Contract Farming:**
 
 
• Farmers may become overly dependent on companies for inputs and technology.
 
• Disputes may arise regarding quality standards, payment delays, or pricing.
 
• Small farmers may face challenges in negotiating favorable contract terms.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Contract Farming in India:**
 
 
• PepsiCo's potato farming initiative in Punjab for its snack products.
 
• Nestle's milk procurement model through direct contracts with dairy farmers.
 
• ITC's e-Choupal initiative for sourcing agricultural produce directly from farmers.

questions.question: According to the Reserve Bank of India, as of October 2024, India became the fourth country whose foreign exchange (forex) reserves swelled to $_______ billion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**701**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• As of October 2024, India became the fourth country in the world to have foreign exchange (forex) reserves exceeding **$701 billion**.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is responsible for managing the country’s forex reserves, which include foreign currency assets, gold reserves, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and the reserve position in the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
 
• India’s forex reserves crossed the $700 billion mark, highlighting its strong economic fundamentals and resilience in the global financial landscape.
 
• Other countries with similar high forex reserves include China, Japan, and Switzerland.
 
• Maintaining high forex reserves is essential for stabilizing the Indian rupee and supporting India’s imports, external debt, and economic growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves**

 
 
• Forex reserves consist of foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs (Special Drawing Rights), and the reserve position in the IMF.
 
• These reserves act as a buffer against external economic shocks and ensure financial stability.
 
• They are critical for maintaining investor confidence and supporting the balance of payments.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**
 
 
• The RBI is India’s central bank, tasked with managing monetary policy, regulating banks, and overseeing the country’s forex reserves.
 
• It actively intervenes in the forex market to stabilize the Indian rupee against global currencies.
 
 
 
• **Special Drawing Rights (SDRs)**

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the functional diversity of RNA molecules in cells?

options.text: Their capability to act as adapter, structural and catalytic molecules
Their permanent role as genetic material
Their ability to form double-stranded helical structures

__
 
• RNA molecules exhibit functional diversity by acting as **adapter molecules** in translation, such as transfer RNA (tRNA), which brings amino acids to the ribosome.
 
• They serve as **structural components** in cellular machinery, such as ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which forms the core of ribosomes.
 
• RNA molecules can act as **catalysts**, such as ribozymes, which facilitate biochemical reactions without being proteins.
 
• RNA plays regulatory roles, such as microRNAs (miRNAs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), which modulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.
 
• The versatility of RNA is due to its ability to adopt complex secondary and tertiary structures, enabling diverse functional roles in cellular processes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Messenger RNA (mRNA):**

 
 
• Acts as a template for protein synthesis during translation.
 
• mRNA carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.
 
• Each mRNA sequence specifies the amino acid sequence of a protein.
 
 
 
• **Transfer RNA (tRNA):**
 
 
• tRNA functions as an adapter molecule in translation.
 
• It has anticodons that pair with mRNA codons and carries specific amino acids to the ribosome.
 
• tRNA’s cloverleaf structure is critical for its role in protein synthesis.
 
 
 
• **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA):**
 
 
• Forms the structural and functional core of ribosomes.
 
• rRNA helps in aligning mRNA and tRNA during translation.
 
• Some rRNA molecules exhibit catalytic activity, facilitating peptide bond formation.
 
 
 
• **Ribozymes:**
 
 
• RNA molecules with enzymatic properties.
 
• Examples include self-splicing introns and the RNA component of RNase P.
 
• Ribozymes demonstrate that RNA can act as both genetic material and a catalyst.

questions.question: How can rivers contribute to the formation of a coastal plain?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By depositing sediments over time**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Rivers contribute to the formation of coastal plains through the process of **sediment deposition** over long periods of time.
 
• As rivers flow, they carry sediments such as sand, silt, and clay, which are deposited at their mouths or along their courses.
 
• These sediments accumulate over time and gradually form flat, low-lying land near the coast, which is referred to as a **coastal plain**.
 
• Examples include the **Eastern Coastal Plains** of India, which were formed by sediment deposition from rivers like the Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri.
 
• The deposition process is influenced by factors such as the river's flow velocity, sediment load, and tidal interactions in coastal areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Coastal Plain:** A flat or gently sloping area of land adjacent to a sea or ocean, often formed by sediment deposition or marine erosion.
 
• **Delta Formation:** In some cases, rivers form deltas at their mouths, where the deposited sediments create triangular landforms, contributing to coastal plain development.
 
• **Alluvium:** Sediments such as sand, silt, and clay transported and deposited by rivers, forming fertile and flat lands.
 
• **Estuaries and Tidal Influence:** In areas where rivers meet the sea, tidal forces can redistribute sediments, further shaping the coastal plain.
 
• **Human Impact:** Human activities such as agriculture, urbanization, and dam construction can alter natural sediment deposition processes, impacting coastal plain formation.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the recent Supreme Court developments on bail under the PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002) in 2024-25?

1. The Supreme Court has clarified that prolonged incarceration without trial can be a valid ground for granting bail under PMLA-2002, despite the twin conditions under Section 45.

2. In Arvind Kejriwal’s case, the Court ruled that the legality of arrest must also consider the “need and necessity” of arrest, in addition to the standard “reasons to believe” clause.

3. The Court has held that “bail is the exception, jail the rule”, which remains applicable in money laundering cases.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2: Statements 1 and 2 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statement 1:** The Supreme Court has clarified that prolonged incarceration without trial can be a valid ground for granting bail under PMLA-2002, despite the twin conditions under Section 45.
 
• **Statement 2:** In a recent judgment related to Arvind Kejriwal’s case, the Court emphasized that the legality of arrest must consider both the "need and necessity" of the arrest and the "reasons to believe" clause.
 
• **Statement 3:** Not correct. The Court did not declare "bail is the exception, jail the rule" as applicable to money laundering cases under PMLA.
 
• The correct interpretation of the Supreme Court’s developments on PMLA bail focuses on ensuring fair trial rights while balancing the stringent provisions of Section 45.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **PMLA, 2002:** The Prevention of Money Laundering Act was enacted to prevent money laundering and confiscate property derived from such activities.
 
• **Section 45:** It imposes twin conditions for granting bail, requiring the court to be satisfied that (1) the accused is not guilty and (2) they are unlikely to commit any offense while on bail.

• **Need and Necessity Test:** Introduced by the Supreme Court, this test evaluates whether an arrest is essential and proportionate, rather than routine, particularly in economic offenses.

questions.question: Prior to 1992, what was the status of Local Governments in India?

options.text: Directly controlled by the Central Government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Statutory status under State Law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Prior to the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments in 1992, Local Governments in India functioned based on **statutory provisions enacted by the respective State Legislatures**.
 
• The Local Government bodies, such as Panchayats and Municipalities, **did not have constitutional recognition** and were established or dissolved at the discretion of state governments.
 
• Local Governments were governed by state-specific laws, resulting in **varying frameworks and powers** across different states.
 
• The absence of constitutional status meant that Local Governments **lacked autonomy** and were primarily dependent on state governments for finances and functional authority.
 
• The 1992 constitutional amendments (73rd and 74th) granted these bodies a **constitutional mandate**, ensuring uniformity, autonomy, and empowerment for self-governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**

 
 
• It granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).
 
• Introduced a three-tier system of Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels.
 
• Mandated regular elections, reservation for women and marginalized groups, and the establishment of the State Election Commission.
 
 
 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**
 
 
• It provided constitutional recognition to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) such as Municipalities.
 
• Defined the structure, composition, and powers of ULBs to ensure urban self-governance.
 
• Introduced provisions for Metropolitan Planning Committees and District Planning Committees.
 
 
 
• **Statutory Status:**
 
 
• Refers to the status granted to institutions or entities through ordinary legislation passed by a legislative body, such as a State Legislature.
 
• Unlike constitutional status, statutory status can be modified or revoked by amending the enabling legislation.
 
 
 
• **Autonomy of Local Governments Post-1992:**
 
 
• Post-1992, Local Governments gained autonomy in decision-making and financial matters.
 
• They were mandated to prepare plans for economic development and social justice as per the Constitution.

questions.question: What term is given, in motivation theory, to the things people value and choose to pursue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Goals**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In motivation theory, the term "goals" refers to the objectives or outcomes that individuals value and actively strive to achieve.
 
• Goals play a critical role in driving human behavior and guiding decision-making, as they provide a sense of direction and purpose.
 
• The concept of setting and pursuing goals is central to several motivation theories, including Goal-Setting Theory by Edwin Locke and Gary Latham.
 
• Clear, challenging, and specific goals are known to enhance motivation, focus, and performance, particularly when paired with feedback and self-monitoring.
 
• Goals can be categorized into short-term, medium-term, and long-term objectives, depending on the timeline and scope of the desired outcome.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Goal-Setting Theory:**

 
 
• Proposed by Edwin Locke in the 1960s, this theory emphasizes the importance of setting specific, challenging goals to increase motivation and performance.
 
• According to the theory, goals must be clear, measurable, and time-bound to be effective.
 
• Providing feedback and recognizing progress are essential elements of successful goal achievement.
 
 
 
• **Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Motivation:**
 
 
• Intrinsic motivation arises from internal factors, such as personal satisfaction or enjoyment derived from the activity itself.
 
• Extrinsic motivation is driven by external rewards, such as money, recognition, or avoiding punishment.
 
• Both types of motivation can influence goal-setting and achievement.
 
 
 
• **Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs:**
 
 
• Abraham Maslow’s theory suggests that human motivation is driven by a hierarchy of needs, starting with basic physiological needs and progressing to self-actualization.
 
• Goals often align with fulfilling these needs, such as financial stability, relationships, or personal growth.
 
 
 
• **SMART Goals:**
 
 
• The SMART framework ensures that goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
 
• This approach is widely used in personal development, education, and organizational management to enhance goal clarity and attainability.
 
 
 
• **Self-Determination Theory (SDT):**
 
 
• SDT emphasizes the role of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in fostering intrinsic motivation and achieving goals.
 
• It highlights the importance of aligning goals with personal values and interests for sustained motivation.

questions.question: Let’s denote Z as the number of atoms per unit cell, M as the molar mass of the substance, and NA as Avogadro’s number. Which formula is used to calculate the density (d) of a unit cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**d = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The formula **d = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA)** is used to calculate the density of a unit cell in crystallography.
 
• In this formula, **Z** represents the number of atoms per unit cell, **M** is the molar mass of the substance, **a³** is the volume of the unit cell (edge length cubed), and **NA** is Avogadro’s number.
 
• The density (d) is expressed in grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³) when the molar mass is in grams per mole and the unit cell volume is in cubic centimeters.

• **Unit Cell:**

 
 
• The unit cell is the smallest repeating structure in a crystal lattice that represents the entire crystal.
 
• Its dimensions are defined by the lengths of edges (a, b, c) and angles between them (α, β, γ).
 
 
 
• **Avogadro’s Number (NA):**
 
 
• Avogadro’s number is approximately **6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹**, representing the number of entities in one mole of a substance.
 
• It is crucial for converting between macroscopic and molecular scales in chemistry.
 
 
 
• **Molar Mass (M):**
 
 
• The molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol).
 
• It is calculated as the sum of the atomic masses of all the elements in a compound.
 
 
 
• **Crystal Lattice:**
 
 
• A crystal lattice is a three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, ions, or molecules in a structured and repeating pattern.
 
• Common types of unit cells include cubic, tetragonal, hexagonal, and orthorhombic systems.
 
 
 
• **Density in Crystals:**
 
 
• Density is a physical property that correlates the mass of a substance to its volume.
 
• In crystallography, density helps determine the packing efficiency and arrangement of atoms within a unit cell.
